options: Split the work across subagents, each given only the tools its role needs.

options: Run /memory to see which memory files the session has loaded.
Nothing is wrong: a subdirectory CLAUDE.md loads when Claude works with files there.

why: Useful for diagnosis, but nothing needs diagnosing: this is expected behavior.
Subdirectory memory loads on demand, so API conventions stay out of web-app work. That's the design working.
Right when a personal file conflicts. Nothing conflicts here.
That would load API conventions into every session, including web-app work where they don't belong.
The cause is already known: the two files conflict.

An on-demand skill, keeping CLAUDE.md for standards that apply to every task.

why: On the exam, allowed-tools limits the tools a skill uses. (Today it pre-approves tools; see Exam vs. today.)

options: Direct execution, since the change is small and the cause is known.
Plan mode, to compare the designs before committing to one.
A planning run whose plan a human approves, then an execution run that applies it.
Delegate exploration to the Explore subagent, then decide what to do.

why: A one-line fix at a known location needs no planning step.
Right when designs compete. There's one obvious fix here.
Right for large automated changes that need consistency. This is one line.
Right when you don't know where to look. The stack trace already points to the line.
Right for small, known changes. Two designs with different infrastructure need comparing first.
Explore both designs against the codebase before committing to either.

Exploration helps, but the core need is comparing two designs before building.
Direct execution is what produces the inconsistency.
Interactive plan mode doesn't fit a nightly job no one is watching.
One approved plan makes every file follow the same choices, and a person signs off before it runs.
Exploring doesn't fix inconsistent choices between files.

options: Describe all the problems together in one message, because the fixes interact.
Give a concrete test case: an input row and the exact expected output.
Have Claude interview you about the requirements before it changes anything.
Report the problems one at a time, because each fix stands alone.

why: When fixes depend on each other, Claude needs to see them together to avoid one breaking another.
Right when a description is misread. Here the bugs interact.
Right when you don't know the requirements. Here the bugs are known.
Right for independent problems. These share one utility.
Right for several interacting problems. Here there's one, repeatedly misread.

Right when the requirement is unknown to you. Here you know what you want.
Right for independent problems. There's one problem here.

options: Pipe the PR's diff into the command and scope the review to those changes.
Run the review in a separate Claude Code invocation from the one that made the fix.
Add --output-format json with --json-schema so the output parses.

options: Add few-shot examples contrasting safe parameterized queries with real concatenation.

Restate the criteria in the prompt with stronger emphasis.
Split the review into separate passes, one for each concern.

Examples of complete findings show the model exactly what to reproduce.

options: Add an "unclear" enum value and route those records to human review.
Return tool output with claim, source, date and excerpt fields.
Make fields that may be absent nullable in the schema.
Force the extraction tool with tool_choice so a call always happens.

Right when findings need structure and attribution. Here the problem is a forced choice.

options: Use synchronous calls, because the deadline is shorter than the batch's worst case.
Use the Message Batches API with a custom_id per item.
Refine the prompt on a small sample before running the full set.
Resubmit only the failed requests, matched by their custom_id.

why: A 15-hour window is shorter than the 24-hour batch worst case, and a miss blocks the release.
Batches can take up to 24 hours. The release can't wait that long.

Right after a batch with failures. Nothing has run yet.

Non-urgent bulk work suits batches at lower cost, and custom_id matches each result to its repository.

options: Have a verification pass score each finding's confidence, with thresholds calibrated on labeled data.
Have a fresh session review the work against specific criteria, without the generator's reasoning.
Review each file in its own pass, then do one pass on cross-file issues.

Right when a reviewer shares the author's blind spots. Here the need is routing.
Right for large diffs. It doesn't sort findings by certainty.
